A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same dataset-properties and membership-inference study. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support comparison, including matching material reorganized between versions.

before.justification: v3 reports original fine-tuning and membership-inference experiments, including Tables A4–A8, plus numerical investigations of the simplified Gaussian model. Results borrowed from earlier studies are identified separately.

after.justification: v4 retains original fine-tuning experiments and adds individual-sample vulnerability measurements in Section 4.4, Figure 6, and Table A10.

M1.justification: The attacks, fine-tuning architectures, and log-linear regression form remain unchanged. v4 extends the prediction procedure to individual vulnerability summaries and adds an inverse calculation mapping a DP-derived TPR target to a predicted minimum number of examples per class (Sections 4.4–4.5 and Appendix E).

E1.justification: All six image datasets and their classification tasks remain. The limited coverage reduction is removal of the numerical Gaussian-model investigations in v3 Table A1 and Figure A.1; the simplified Gaussian construction remains as theory. The new individual analysis uses the existing Patch Camelyon dataset.

E2.justification: The LiRA/RMIA comparison, alternative log(TPR) regression, and Head/FiLM/from-scratch comparisons retain their comparator membership. Table 1 introduces an analytical DP-bound yardstick, rather than results from an additional attack or DP-trained comparison model.

E3.justification: v4 adds per-example evaluation using 257 rotating target/shadow models at FPR=0.1, including intermediate shot counts 23170 and 49152. It also specifies C=2, delta=0.00001, and selected epsilon values for the new extrapolation analysis. Existing training splits, tuning budgets, and backbone configurations are retained.

E4.justification: Sections 4.4–4.5 add substantial analyses of whether increasing dataset size protects the most vulnerable samples, using maxima, vulnerability quantiles, and extrapolation against DP bounds. Conversely, v3's numerical RMIA bound-gap check and small-FPR approximation diagnostic are removed. The alternative regression and cross-backbone analyses remain.

E5.justification: The new individual-vulnerability analysis reports medians and raw minimum/maximum values over six seeds. Existing aggregate Clopper–Pearson intervals, six- or twelve-seed summaries, and regression confidence intervals remain unchanged. This adds an uncertainty-reporting practice without establishing an increase in existing experiments' run counts.

E6.justification: Matched image-dataset tables and retained regression rows are numerically unchanged. v4 adds quantile slopes near -0.5 versus a maximum-vulnerability slope of -0.2695, and Table 1's extrapolated sample requirements, including 7 million worst-case examples per class at epsilon=1 and FPR=0.1. Regression results at FPR=0.0001 and 0.00001 and the earlier Gaussian numerical diagnostics are removed.

T1.justification: v4 replaces isotropic covariance s²I with general covariance Sigma and adds an explicit asymptotic remainder to the LiRA theorem. It revises the RMIA lemma to use a folded distribution and absolute-value expectations, replaces the former power-law inequality with an approximation and expanded asymptotic reasoning, and adds the DP-bound inversion in Appendix E. These are substantive mathematical revisions beyond relocating proofs.

C1.justification: The power-law and regression claims remain, but v4 makes empirical worst-case vulnerability and the extremely large dataset requirements for protecting vulnerable samples central contributions. Its abstract and introduction also explicitly foreground LiRA optimality in the simplified model and the relationship between empirical MIA evaluation and DP.

C2.justification: v3 discusses using vulnerability predictions to assess privacy risks and when DP might be necessary. v4 emphasizes that the required dataset sizes limit practical protection and reinforce the importance of formal DP guarantees. It adds distributional qualifications and distinguishes its DP-bound comparison from actual DP training, while removing the earlier small-FPR discrepancy explanation and imbalance/outlier future-work discussion.

D1.justification: Backbone access instructions, dataset versions, hyperparameter ranges, and compute disclosures are retained. v4 adds the calculation recipe for Table 1 and a plan to publish code after acceptance; this does not establish public code availability. Removing the synthetic diagnostics also removes their specific simulation settings.

R1.justification: v4 substantially broadens its positioning around disparate vulnerability, generalization, and worst-case membership inference, adding works including Kulynych, Guépin, and Azize and Basu. Neyman–Pearson optimality and Kairouz's DP bounds support the revised framing. The reconstruction-attack references to Balle and Nasr are removed.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, contribution list, and discussion are extensively rewritten. RMIA background and theory are consolidated in an appendix, uncertainty estimation moves into the background, and the appendices are reorganized with a contents page. The author block and terminology also change.

P2.justification: The original two-panel Figure 1 becomes separate figures placed in the introduction and experimental section. v4 adds Figure 6 and Tables 1/A10, removes the earlier Gaussian diagnostic displays, trims regression displays to three FPR values, and adds theoretical reference lines. Typography and figure placement change throughout the document.

improvement.justification: v4 adds useful individual-risk evidence and clarifies the distinction from DP guarantees. However, it removes informative very-low-FPR results and diagnostics, while introducing unresolved issues: Equation (11) appears to omit a required ||x|| factor in its Cauchy–Schwarz bound, and Table A10 labels the corresponding Figure 6 TPR−FPR values as TPR. These affect support and clarity for the newly emphasized worst-case claims, leaving the net quality direction uncertain.
